analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising fee per ton of carbon and pays the money to every taxpayer.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have charged fossil fuel producers for every ton of carbon and mailed the proceeds to taxpayers, died in committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require coal producers, oil refiners, and the first sellers of natural gas to buy a federal permit for each ton of carbon dioxide their fuel would emit, with prices starting around $6–19 per ton in 2015 and climbing to at least $119 per ton by 2024. All of the money would go into a trust fund and be paid out in equal monthly dividends to lawful U.S. residents, with any remainder used to reduce the federal deficit. Because every resident gets the same dividend but wealthier households use more energy, most lower- and middle-income families would come out ahead financially, while fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users would pay more.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawful U.S. resident would receive an equal monthly dividend from the permit revenue. Lower- and middle-income households would typically receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel prices, since they use less energy than average. The deficit would shrink with any leftover revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers, via equal monthly dividends

how_it_helps.text: The bill deposits all permit revenue into an Energy and Economic Security Trust Fund and requires the Treasury to pay monthly dividends to every lawful resident, splitting shares among joint filers and paying half-shares for up to two dependents [S2][S3].

Permit prices rise on a fixed schedule from a $6.25–$18.75 range in 2015 to at least $106.25 per ton by 2023, giving companies decades of predictable price signals to shift toward cleaner energy rather than a sudden shock [S2][S3].
A border fee on carbon-intensive imports and rebates to exporters are designed to keep U.S. manufacturers from being undercut by countries without similar carbon pricing [S2][S3].

Emissions targets in the bill call for cutting U.S. greenhouse gas emissions to 20% of 2005 levels by the 2055–2059 period, with intermediate targets of 70% by 2025–2029 and 50% by 2035–2039 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers, oil refiners, natural gas first sellers, and importers of carbon-intensive goods would pay permit fees that rise every year, costs they would pass through in fuel and goods prices. Wealthier households and heavy energy users would pay more in added costs than they receive in dividends.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: Energy prices would rise for everyone before dividends arrive; households with high heating or driving costs, including many rural and working families, could pay more than they receive in dividends despite the equal per-person payout [S2][S3].
The Treasury, not a market, sets the permit price and can raise it further if emissions targets are missed, which could push costs higher than scheduled if reductions fall short [S2][S3].

An economy-wide price on carbon would hit energy-intensive industries like steel, cement, glass, and chemicals, and the bill's export rebates and import fees would need to work as designed to prevent job losses and offshoring [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is a straightforward trade: pay more for fossil energy, get an equal per-person dividend that more than offsets the cost for most households, and let rising prices steadily push the economy off coal and oil. The dividend structure is genuinely progressive, and the long phase-in limits the shock. The main honest concerns are near-term price increases for energy-heavy households and regions, and the risk that a Treasury-set price misjudges either emissions or economic pain, since a price that misses its targets can be raised.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single representative with no cosponsors, referred to two committees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the bill on May 28, 2014 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, for portions within its jurisdiction, the Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
Days later it was referred to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 without the bill ever coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers avoided a rising per-ton carbon fee, and no dividend payments were ever made; the status quo on both energy prices and emissions continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; no dividends were ever paid

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only supporter in the record is a single Democrat, and no Republican or Democratic colleague signed on.

industries.note: Coal would face the highest per-ton permit charges of any fuel because it emits the most carbon dioxide when burned, and the fixed price schedule makes those costs mandatory and rising. Coal companies' interest in avoiding the fee runs against the bill's dividends and emissions cuts.

Refinery operators would pay a permit for every ton of carbon in the petroleum products they process, with prices rising yearly. The industry's savings from blocking the bill come at the expense of the dividend payments the public would have received.
First sellers of natural gas would pay permits too, but gas emits less carbon than coal or oil, so the bill would improve its competitive position against dirtier fuels even as it adds costs.

These industries would face higher energy and feedstock costs, but the bill rebates the equivalent cost to exporters and imposes a matching fee on carbon-intensive imports, shielding them from competitors in countries without carbon pricing.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel consumers, including utilities and transportation
industries.note: Any business burning coal, oil products, or natural gas would pass permit costs into electricity, gasoline, and heating prices, with the dividend as the offset for households.
